title: Fabric Lakehouse vs Data Warehouse: Best Practices
summary: A community blog post walking through when to choose a Fabric Lakehouse versus a Fabric Warehouse, framed as a decision tree (dev-tooling fit, transactional needs, data shape) rather than a size-based choice, plus notes on how the two engines interoperate inside one workspace.
audience: Fabric architects and data engineers choosing or mixing Lakehouse and Warehouse items within a medallion architecture.
why_it_matters: Teams often default to Lakehouse-only or Warehouse-only designs; this source captures the cross-engine interop constraints (read-only SQL endpoint, no Spark writes to Warehouse tables, RLS-mode conflicts) that force a mixed 'better together' pattern in practice.
takeaways: Engine choice should follow team tooling (T-SQL vs Spark) and transactional needs, not data volume.
Lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint is read-only, so multi-table T-SQL writes require a Warehouse.
Spark cannot write directly to Warehouse tables — Lakehouse-then-INSERT/SELECT is the standard bridge pattern.
OneLake keeps both engines on the same Delta Parquet files, so mixed Lakehouse+Warehouse designs share one storage layer and one capacity cost pool.
Applying security at the wrong layer (T-SQL RLS vs semantic-model RLS) has different downstream effects for each engine.

claims.text: The choice between Lakehouse and Warehouse is best framed as which development tooling the team already uses (Spark/PySpark vs T-SQL) and what transactional guarantees the Gold layer needs, rather than a decision driven by data size.
Every Fabric Lakehouse auto-provisions a read-only SQL analytics endpoint, so multi-table T-SQL DML is not possible against a Lakehouse directly.

Spark notebooks in Fabric cannot write directly to Warehouse tables (no Warehouse target for saveAsTable-style writes); the standard bridge pattern is for Spark to write to a Lakehouse table and have the Warehouse pull it in via INSERT...SELECT.

Fabric supports cross-database queries between a Lakehouse and Warehouse in the same workspace using three-part naming (database.schema.table), which is how a Gold-layer Warehouse commonly reads Silver-layer Lakehouse tables.

Lakehouse and Warehouse items in the same capacity both store data as Delta Parquet in OneLake and draw from the same F-SKU capacity unit pool, so there is no separate storage choice or separate pricing tier between the two engines.

The post reports a known compatibility issue where OneLake's workspace-level security roles (OneSecurity) do not work together with Direct Lake semantic models built on the same Lakehouse, as of mid-2026.

A recommended medallion pattern keeps Bronze and Silver layers in a Lakehouse for Spark-based ETL/CDC/feature engineering, while the Gold layer is built either as Lakehouse materialized views or as a Warehouse with T-SQL star schemas, with the Warehouse reading Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries.

Row-level security is recommended at the semantic-model layer for Power BI consumption, while T-SQL-layer row-level security in the Warehouse is reserved for direct Warehouse access by non-Power-BI clients, since the two security layers behave differently for downstream reporting.
